utterances.text: I'm not that acquainted with our legal provisions. With regard to whether you have to be 14 or 16 I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How about getting a driver's licence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have to be 18 to drive a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How about to vote?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: What about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What about voting? Can she vote at 14?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you can't vote at age 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You've got to be 18; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you do to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And she can't enter in a contract, can she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At age 14, as far as I know -- well, it all depends what contracts. If I go into a department store as a 12-year-old, I buy something and I get a receipt. That's a kind of contract, if you will, but as regard to the legal details, I'd rather not go into them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Can she consent to surgery?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Consent to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Consent to surgery.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So just because she was over 14, she can't vote, can't drive a car, you don't know about marrying, you don't know about consent to surgery, but she's not a child under your legal system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. She is what they call Strafmundig, that is to say that she would have to assume responsibility for any crimes or offences she committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. So the only thing that can happen to her, the only way she is treated as an adult is --let me follow that a little bit further. If a 14 year old person, be it Sanda Mucic or my 14 year old daughter, were charged with a crime in Austria, a serious crime, would that person go to the same court you and I would?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person -- there's the adolescent court, if you will, that would be competent, the juvenile court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That person wouldn't, if they were convicted of a crime, wouldn't go to the same penitentiary that someone who was 30 year old would go to for the same crime, would they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So she's not really an adult, is she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At 14 she's not an adult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So she's still a child under your legal system; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She's a child up to age 14. After that she is a juvenile or an adolescent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. So she's treated just like an adult from the age of 14 over?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When does somebody -- never mind. Strike that. Detective, you put a lot of overtime in on watching all these videotapes and things, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you did that because somebody from the Tribunal asked you to do it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that isn't right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You just did it because it seemed like a good idea at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a court order from an Austrian court and we acted on that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Your Honour, if I can just have a second while I go through my notes, I think I'm about done. While you were in police school, basic police school, back in 1981-1984, did they teach you to write reports that correctly reflected what had actually occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that then in practice that's what you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Because people rely on those reports, don't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rely? Well, when objects are seized for the court, --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid the interpreter didn't catch the last bit of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What I'm saying is the people rely on the facts in those reports to make decisions, don't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you want those reports to be correct, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And I'll bet you when you were in detective school from October 1991-October 1992 they taught you the same thing, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that's standard training for Austrian police officers, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, you say you are a member of the Austrian Federal Police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So that would be the equivalent of the Federal Bureau of Investigation from my country, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that any straightforward comparison would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. But you are the national police force enforcing national law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With regard to the Federal Police divisions, in Vienna there is Division 1 through Division 5. Division 1, in which I work, were responsible for crimes in the political sphere. Division 2 deals with normal offences such as theft, drug dealing. That's what Division 2 does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you are a political police officer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That may not be the right thing to say. He deals with political offences. It doesn't mean he is a political police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me rephrase that, your Honour. I appreciate that. I think I may have misphrased it. You're part of the security organs of the state; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a detective with the Federal Police in Vienna. I work in Division 1. That is the office for the protection of the state of individuals and of property. That is the area I work in. I belong to the detective unit which means that at any time I could be working as a detective somewhere else. It's just the way the offences are broken down, that we do have this category of political offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. A couple of other quick things. At the time Pavo Mucic was arrested he was given a document in German called information sheet for arrested persons, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now with regard to that being handed over, I didn't see that happen, but I do know that he got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it was handed to him in German; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document was handed over in German and in the record that is noted down and also the interpreter was present at the time. It is signed by the suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Was it explained to him in a language he understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not present when the explanations were given or at least I didn't pay any heed while the explanations were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you don't know whether or not his rights under Austrian law were explained to him in Croatian, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was present when this was explained to him by his daughter in the apartment. Now, at the police headquarters I don't know exactly how this was done by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you were there when it was explained to him by his daughter, who's not old enough to drive a car or vote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few days before that we spoke to Mr. Mucic in Germany and we knew that Mucic spoke German, because he had had dealings with the police in 1991, and the record, the Niederschrift, had been filled out, which was forwarded to the court, and as far as I knew and as far as I could see, Mr. Mucic was aware of the grounds of the arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. You have testified at some point that your English is about as good as his German; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. What was as good as his German?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That Detective Moerbauer's English is about as good as Pavo's German?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's good grounds for comparison, yes. That means it's good enough to get by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Could this be handed to the witness and marked? While that's being done, let me ask you a question. This document, information sheets for arrested persons, that's there to inform --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, can we have a break now for lunch?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Three minutes, Judge, and I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. And that document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, did you notice that Mr. Mucic was able to point out that the German translation was not correct yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That was Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Oh, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What was the marking on that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Detective Moerbauer, when that document is handed to you, without the help of the interpreter, I want you to read it, just the yellow highlighted part, and tell the judges what it means. I'm here to tell you that that is a correct explanation of law from another country.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to this. I can't see where it's leading at all in terms of -- if counsel is trying to establish the proficiency of the witness' English, then I hardly see how it is relevant to any of the matters that he has raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think an issue before us is whether or not Pavo Mucic understood his rights under Austrian law, as explained to him in the information sheet for arrested persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But, your Honours, in my submission none of this took place in the English language. So what is the relevance of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gschwendt was asked a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This information document. Mr. Gschwendt was asked about these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was asked the content of the documents, not about Mr. Mucic's understanding of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may just correct the record, I believe that Mr. Gschwendt said they were all interpreted to the accused in his own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Also, your Honour, having looked over my notes a little bit further, Moran's iron clad law on time by lawyers seems to be coming into play now. I do have a little bit more. It might be better if we went to lunch now. Again that iron clad law, I made a good faith estimate and I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you continuing after lunch?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We will now break for lunch. (1.00 pm) (Luncheon Adjournment) 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 (2.30 pm) (Witness re-enters court) (Interpreter re-enters court)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Apologies to the court. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Apologies, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: You are still under oath I might remind you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I'll just pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Moerbauer, I want to ask you now some questions please in connection with this matter. Can I just ask you this, please, Mr. Moerbauer? I'm not entirely clear as to what your police unit actually does. That is Abteilung 1, it's called, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Abteilung 1 is for the protection of the State, of individuals and of property. Now protection of the State, this has to do with offences which in the criminal code are considered to be political in nature; for example, a threat to neutrality is referred to. Then there is matters relating to Yugoslavia; in connection with violations of the UN embargo, etc. So it's those kinds of dealings that our division is involved in. Then in the case of people whose lives are in danger or when there's official visits, we provide protection there. Then there's also objects in connection with international organisations, which Division 1, which I work for, is in charge of protecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So it involves a wider range than counter-espionage, counter-subversion and counter-terrorism, a wider remit than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Is your unit considered to be an elite unit within the Austrian police force, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Division 1 is one that reports to the Vienna Police Department. It's on the same footing as Divisions 2 through 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I ask you now, please, about your training as a detective? You've answered some questions about that, but I would like just a little more detail, please. When you are trained to be a detective, is one of the things that you are trained in how to prepare for the conduct of an interview with a suspect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And amongst the things that you are taught is no doubt to assemble all the witness statements in a particular case, to study them before you go and interview someone; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not right. Anyone who is arrested, after arrest is questioned, a record is kept, and on that occasion he has an opportunity to state his views as to the reasons for which he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But when you interview a suspect, Mr. Moerbauer, how do you know what questions to ask him, if you haven't found out what the case is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the arrest warrant was issued on specific grounds and the record of the interview is taken on the basis of that warrant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about the information which you had prior to the arrest of Mr. Mucic in early March of 1996. You first became aware of this case on 6th March, when you were on holiday; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And it was sufficiently important for your colleague, Mr. Panzer, to telephone you whilst you were on holiday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What rank is Mr. Panzer, by the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Panzer has the same rank as I do. He's District Inspector, and he's also a team or unit leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So by the time that you came to arrest Mr. Mucic, is this right, that you had become aware of three potential claimants for him: this Tribunal, the former Republic of Yugoslavia, and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware that there were three bodies involved: the Austrian court, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The only one that was accompanied by any degree of detailed information, that was the Tribunal's request, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information I saw was provided by 210, Department 210, Interpol, in other words one document. There were only two or three pages. In that document was stated that Mucic was suspected as camp commander of Celebici of having committed crimes and on the basis of that document I acquired my knowledge. So Department 210 should have more information and, in fact, I was given some other information, more details, from Department 210.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But was that document which you saw an international criminal Tribunal document, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw one document, as best I can remember, from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And you had no information from any other source aside from that document and the arrest warrant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The further information was provided to me from the people in Department 210.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How extensive was that information, Mr. Moerbauer? Was it a two minute conversation or a ten minute conversation or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a conversation that was relatively short. I was informed that he was allegedly camp commander in Celebici and that there had been mistreatment of prisoners there, and that people had been locked up in shafts, and that's what I knew and that's all I knew until we began with the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of the requests that were being made for extradition of Mr. Mucic, the only one that caused people to be present was the one from the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, in our department there was no contact with other investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So that the only people who turned up to pursue their request for this man was this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, people from other organs or from other courts I don't have any knowledge of there being any.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The answer is this, isn't it: there were no other representatives from any other body other than the International Tribunal pursuing Mr. Mucic actively before and after his arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would now like to turn to the day of his arrest, Mr. Moerbauer, 18th March, 2.15 in the afternoon, but prior to 2.15 in the afternoon had you and your colleagues been making observations at the Taubergasse area all that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Moerbauer, I don't want to know where your observation post was, but I want to know this, please. Did the observation post that you had have a good clear view of the Taubergasse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, on that day Mr. Mucic was repairing a car in the Natagasse and it was, in fact, a colleague who went up to him and talked to him about the repairing of the car. In fact, that lasted a fair bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you help me about this. Can you recall at what time he was first seen that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know that it was in the course of the morning, but I'm afraid I can't tell you the precise time. I'd have to have a look at the relevant document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, just help us. I mean, are we talking early morning, mid-morning, closer to lunchtime? What are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 11 o'clock, closer to noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And so at the time he was arrested, 2.15, he was still working on this vehicle in the Natagasse, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he repaired the car, went into the apartment, came back to the vehicle, went on fixing it. At the time of the arrest he'd already fixed the car. He was on his way to -- if the interpreter has understood it rightly -- to the Suzuki car shop. That's when he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: At what time had you started making observations that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The observation began at around 7 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And whilst he was in the Natagasse did you continue to keep watch on the Taubergasse address?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several people scattered around this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And Mr. Mucic was quite alone at the time of his arrest, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic was alone at the time of his arrest, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And physically I think you and your colleague, Mr. Panzer, were the two that actually went and arrested him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Panzer, Bycek, Borlak and myself were present at the scene and two officers secured the area and Panzer and myself went ahead with the arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Immediately upon his arrest, and by that I mean there in the street, you say that he was told of his rights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was informed of the grounds of the arrest?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He needed an interpreter throughout these proceedings, didn't he, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The interpreter was at police headquarters as of 4 o'clock and the questioning of the suspect and the filling in of the forms at police headquarters was carried out in the presence of an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You see, I suggest to you, Mr. Moerbauer, that the reality is that Mr. Mucic doesn't have a very good understanding of German, and you're not being entirely straight with us when you say he does.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic certainly understood the grounds of the arrest and he also understood the further proceedings, and he also, in fact, mentioned that he had been expecting the police to turn up for a number of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If he understood what you were saying to him, why did you need to get his 16 year old daughter to explain it to him in the flat then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because Mr. Mucic apparently on account of the circumstances was a bit overwhelmed, a bit too overwhelmed to express himself in German.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I suggest to you that the reality was that he hadn't understood what he'd been told outside because his German was not up to it, Mr. Moerbauer. That's why you needed to get someone else to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With regard to the grounds, whether he understood that on the spot, well, I can't claim anything there, but by the time we got to the apartment it was clear to him exactly what was going on and why these measures had been taken in his respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look at this document, please. There's a copy for the Prosecution and a copy for you. (Handed to Prosecution). (Handed to witness). Can you see that document, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the record, and I'm sorry if I murder the German language while I do it, Mr. Moerbauer, it's entitled "Anhaltemeldung"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is an Anhaltemeldung.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would that be a custody report? Would that be a fair translation of that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is notification that the arrest has been carried out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The arrest report the interpreter might suggest might be closer, arrest record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you like to look at the last page, please? Do you see some signatures there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is one of those signatures your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is on this Anhaltemeldung, but I do not recognise my initials there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I apologise for it being an indistinct copy, Mr. Moerbauer, but is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not the way I usually sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution may have the original of this document, and I would ask whether they can possibly produce the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We have a certified copy of the official judicial file, so probably a better photocopy. The original is in Austria.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am grateful to my learned friend Mr. Turone for that information. Perhaps we could see the certified copy, because it's quite an important document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can ask him whether he remembers signing this document or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour is going to take the next question out of my mouth but I want to be as fair to him as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In any case this is a certified copy, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In the process of photocopying sometimes signatures become less distinct. I want to be as fair to him as possible. I am going to ask him some questions about this document. I don't want there to be any unfairness to him: (Handed to witness). Is that any better, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is better. With regard to this Anhaltemeldung, I recognise it, but this is not my usual signature, the way I usually put my initials on a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Help me about this, Mr. Moerbauer. You were in charge of this detachment, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was involved in the arrest and as far as I know what is stated in this arrest record is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You recall the document, do you, or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember the document, yes, the Anhaltemeldung.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would just like you to read to yourself the whole document. Don't read it out aloud. Just read it to yourself so that you refresh your memory, please. Just dealing with your signature, you're saying that's not your signature in effect; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not the way I sign or initial usually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So are you saying that someone else forged your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't rule that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It would have to be one of your colleagues, wouldn't it, who forged your signature on that document, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who signed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Who else would have access to that document before it was signed, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Theoretically any persons who were on the premises after the arrest and the search. All the records and reports are drawn up that are needed at once, as these records and reports are sent to the court on the same day or the following day, that is to say when the suspect was handed over to the prison facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Are you telling us that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. It is an official document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an arrest record, an Anhaltemeldung. It notifies that Zdravko Mucic was arrested and how the arrest was carried out and what the grounds for the arrest were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Are you telling us, Mr. Moerbauer, that anyone could wander into your office and sign a document on your behalf just like that? Are you really telling us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point in time the only people who came into the office at police headquarters were the officers involved in the search and arrest, and I might add that the people from the Tribunal were present, but I don't believe that the Anhaltemeldung, the arrest record, was ready at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, let us just have a look at something contained in that document. Can I just ask you to re-read again, please, the second page of that document, and to assist you to find the place, it's line eight, Mr. Moerbauer, that's line eight from the top: I think the sentence starts: "Unmittelbar". Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You have already told us that the contents of this document are true. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Correct me if the translation which has been provided by the Prosecution is incorrect, but I'll read out so as to assist you. It says this, doesn't it: "Immediately upon his arrest Zdravko Mucic was informed of the crime he was suspected of having committed and of the grounds of the arrest warrant". That was in the street, wasn't it? That's what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The report refers to what happened in the apartment. Upon arrest he had already been informed and he was informed once again in the apartment about the grounds of the arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Forgive me, Mr. Moerbauer. What do the words "immediately upon his arrest" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means immediately after the grounds for the arrest were made aware to him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In fact, if the interpreter might add, it does say in the German "Unmittelbar nach", "immediately after the arrest", for what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am grateful for that assistance and I don't pursue the point. Let's go on to the next point. He was handcuffed and he complained about the nature of the handcuffing, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The handcuffs were put on a bit too tight upon arrest, but the handcuffs were taken off his hands, because initially he had had the handcuffs put on his hands behind his back and in the apartment they were opened and then he had his hands cuffed again in the front somewhat looser.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: They had caused quite a bit of a mark, hadn't they, quite a bit of a reddening and injury to the wrist, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The wrist was irritated, red from irritation, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Now as far as what happened in the house is concerned, what I suggest to you, Mr. Moerbauer, is only Mr. Mucic was present in the house at the beginning of this procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, when we began with the search itself, his daughter was already present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, you told us in evidence yesterday -- you told us that, but you also concede, when Ms. Residovic was asking you questions, that she may have come in later. I suggest she came in as late as 3 o'clock, Mr. Moerbauer. ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The daughter of Mucic was there when Mr. Mucic was informed of the grounds of arrest in the apartment and acted as interpreter. Thereupon we began with the search.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, I suggest she came in at 3.00 and she was obviously a schoolgirl. She had all her -- she came in from school that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only say that when we began with the search Sanda Mucic was already present in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, the search lasted three-quarters of an hour or thereabouts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About three-quarters of an hour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Look at line 25 of page 2 of your document, please, Mr. Moerbauer. I think you'll find it's the final paragraph on that page. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Again allowing for the translation being incorrect, would you agree that it says this: "In 1170 Vienna, Taubergasse 15, Door 10 and in the other premises belonging thereto, in the time from 14:20 to 15:40 hours, in the presence of Zdravko Mucic and his daughter, Sanda Mucic, the court ordered house search was carried out"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Whatever it may say in the Niederschrift, in that document you are saying that the search came to an end at 1540 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now it was 1540 when the search was over, when we locked the door. That wasn't cleared up yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: With the search ending at 1540 and having lasted about three-quarters of an hour, that timing would fit with Sanda Mucic coming in at 3 o'clock, wouldn't it, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sanda Mucic acted as interpreter to inform him of his rights and afterwards that's when we began with the search. Now, as to exactly down to the last minute that was, I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you help me about this, please: was Taubergasse 15, Door 14, one of the other premises you were referring to in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was another search, Taubergasse 15, Door 14, and as far as I know, Sanda Mucic was present there as a witness, according to the relevant document, the Sicherstellungs Protokoll.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So the search of Taubergasse 15, Door 14, would also have been completed by 1540 hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The time as to when the search began and ended at Taubergasse 15/14, the time indicated in the Sicherstellungs Protokoll, in the search record, is not familiar to me. I can't tell you what time was put down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You've just used the name of a document that I'm not familiar with. What document is that, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Sicherstellungs Protokoll is the form that you use during a house search. These are the documents that bore the wrong date. They have had the 19th March 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What we've been calling the Niederschrift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If the Niederschrift for Taubergasse 15, Door 14, says the search came to an end at 1610, that's the definitive one, is it, the definitive time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the officers put that time down, that must have been the time. As to whether that was the time at which the search was ended or the time at which the apartment was locked up, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So the information contained in the custody report that you've told us was true isn't true, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now the time of the search in Taubergasse 15, Door 10, at 2.15 Mucic was arrested. We went to the apartment. It takes at most five minutes. So by 2.20 in the afternoon the apartment should have been opened and that time should be about right. Now that the search was over by 3.40 in the afternoon, the search may have been over earlier than that, but that the apartment was locked or left only later, as I say, at 1540 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Forgive me, Mr. Moerbauer. The Niederschrift and the custody report have different ending times for this procedure, don't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, I do not know what time is indicated in the Niederschrift.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Have a look at D53/1, please, which I think is in the possession of the Registry. Do you see the bottom line there, Mr. Moerbauer. 16:10 hours, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the search of Taubergasse 15, Door 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In your custody record you have said that the words "other premises" includes Taubergasse 15, Door 14 and you've said in that report the search is ended at 15.40 hours. They cannot both be true, can they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Anhaltemeldung it says at the apartment Door 10 the search lasted from 2.20 in the afternoon until 3.40 in the afternoon. In the Niederschrift it says for Door 14 the relevant documents were handed over in connection with that apartment at 4.10 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Now would you like to answer my question, please. They can't both be right, can they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now the search of Taubergasse 15, Door 10, ended at 3.30. There were some 20 minutes to go ahead with the search of Taubergasse 15, Door 14. I don't see any contradiction there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Moerbauer. We'll move on. You treated Sanda Mucic as a person of confidence for the purposes of search and interpretation and so on, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sanda Mucic was not used as a person of confidence at Taubergasse 15, Door 10. Rather, as the search warrant -- the search warrants, rather, all related to Mucic and he lived at Door 10, no person of confidence was used for the search. Sanda Mucic was indeed present, but with regard to the Niederschrift, she didn't sign that. Now I don't know if she was present during this search at Taubergasse 15, Door 10 throughout, because she was present during the search at Taubergasse 15, Door 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Having received information that this man was wanted for war crimes, did you do a check on his background, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These checks were carried out, because in the initial information was simply a request by the court to gather information, which was passed on to us via Interpol.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And amongst that information that you checked, having initiated this inquiry, did you check on the number of children that he'd got?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was ascertained who was registered with the police as living in the apartment. There were two minors there, who were registered as living there. Now as to whether they were the children of Mr. Mucic or not was not ascertained specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You knew he'd got some children, Mr. Moerbauer, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There was a reasonable chance that the minors referred to living at that address were going to be his children; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now when we initially made contact at Door 10, the first thing we saw, Mr. Mucic -- we saw the daughter. We did not on that occasion see his son and it could not be ruled out that these individuals might not be living there in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You'd had this place under observation for how long, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall we began on 14th March with the observation. First, it was on a small scale and then there were additional officers involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And no doubt because you were interested in not just Mr. Mucic's apartment but other apartments in there, you'd been keeping a note of exactly who had been coming and going, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No list was kept of who went in or out. There was just Zdravko Mucic and Zejnil Delalic who were the focus with a view to arresting them at an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You see, I suggest to you, Mr. Moerbauer, you knew full well this girl was a minor, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now whether the girl was a minor or not, that's something that was given very little attention. With regard to the investigations, they were about Zdravko Mucic and not about his daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: This was the girl you were using as an interpreter to explain that he was being arrested for war crimes, Mr. Moerbauer. Are you saying to this Tribunal that you didn't care what age she was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The girl gave the impression that she understood everything full well and she was also able to translate the circumstances to him, because you're not talking about that small a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: We're talking about someone of the age who was not allowed to vote, not allowed to do all the sort of things that were adult things to do, Mr. Moerbauer, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. Asked and answered already.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would be very grateful if the flow of my cross-examination is not interrupted, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objections are not interruptions, your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You know, because you were able to have a conversation about her being taken into the care of the social services, that she was 16 years old, didn't you, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was at the end of the search. That's when that issue was addressed with Mr. Mucic, what should become of the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let's now talk about the Niederschrift that were obtained in this case, Mr. Moerbauer. The purpose of those documents is what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose of the document is to be consistent with the legal provisions. You have to keep these documents. You have to put down the date when the search took place, who conducted the search, who was involved in the search and what the grounds for the search was and what objects were seized.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It's not just a form that you can fill out just like that. It's a very important document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Niederschrift is a form and would be possible to fill it out entirely in handwriting without any part of it having been typed beforehand, but it is a very important document without question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the documents about which you were asked yesterday, those contain serious errors as to dates, don't they, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were mistakes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And Mr. Mucic on one occasion was asked to sign a form concerning a search at which he had not been present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now in a Niederschrift there's the possibility for any person signing it to make corrections to it. That's why, had he spotted the mistake, he might have brought that to attention. That's a normal procedure, to make changes to a Niederschrift.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He can't make corrections about something he hasn't witnessed, can he, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Niederschrift which Mr. Mucic signed in connection with Taubergasse 15, Door 10, that Niederschrift was drawn up at police headquarters in Vienna and at that time an interpreter was already present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Now would you like to answer the question that I asked you, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The search I carried out in Taubergasse 15, Door 10, Mr. Mucic was present and as far as this record, this form goes, he signed that at police headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let's move on. There were errors in the recording of quantities of property recovered. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The errors regarding the videotapes were corrected. There were notes entered into the record and when it comes to seizing the -- when it comes to the searches during which the mistakes were made, I was not present at those searches.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would the three most important facts to be recorded in a Niederschrift be these: the date, the person present at the search and the property recovered during the search? Would those be the three most important facts to be recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So in respect of those three most important facts, there are errors in these documents. That's right, isn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And inaccuracy renders these documents unreliable as to what happened on 18th March. Would you agree with that, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, after the objects had been seized for the Austrian court, that means they are -- can be used for evidence, and it's for the court to decide whether that will be the case or not. Now, the fact of the matter is that an error was made. Whenever you have something on a larger scale like this, mistakes can and do happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But, as you've conceded, these weren't minor mistakes, were they, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now the extent to which these errors impact on things, that's something for the court to decide. Now, the form should have been given the right date. I acknowledge that, but the mistake happened. Everybody signed the document. Nobody noticed that a mistake had been made, and before signing, everyone had an opportunity to make corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How would you characterise the quality of the record-keeping of Abteilung 1 on 18th March of last year, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Niederschriften usually are done quite thoroughly, as is everything else. Operations are carried out on the basis of the laws in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The only thing that was thoroughly done on this occasion was to make a thorough shambles of your record-keeping. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this. Your Honour, this question doesn't call for an answer and in my submission counsel is putting words into the witness' mouth. He said already that the witness agreed that the record-keeping was less than satisfactory and there was such agreement from the witness at all stages. I submit this question merely amounts to arguing with the witness and is progressing the matter no further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that's a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Moerbauer, to his arrival at police headquarters. What time was it that he arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived between 4.30 and 5.00 in the afternoon. That's when we reached the Vienna police headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this right, that as far as you were concerned Mr. Mucic was your prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not my prisoner. He had been arrested pursuant to a court-issued warrant of arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Who is in charge of him, Mr. Moerbauer? It cannot be nobody, can it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now with regard to responsibility for the arrest, that lies with the officers carrying it out. This goes for the way the arrest is carried out, acting consistent to the legal provisions and acting in conformity with the Code of Criminal Procedure. Now, the responsibility is with the senior most officer involved in the operation. So he is in charge of supervising the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Who was in charge of supervising Mr. Mucic, not the operation, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the office at police headquarters Mr. Gschwendt was present. He's an officer in Division 1. He had the responsibility there. Now with regard to the activities outside the headquarters, the team leader was my colleague, Panzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So is the answer to the question that Mr. Gschwendt was in charge, physically in charge of Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First Lieutenant Gschwendt at the time was responsible for the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Who put him in Room 331, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was along and brought him to Room 331 but I can't say who else was along, whether it was Panzer. It may also have been Borlak or Bycek who went upstairs from the car with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Who was responsible for his safety and his security as a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both officers were responsible for the security, the two officers who were along with him. The seniormost officer is in charge, but with regard to the prisoner, both officers are responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Are they also responsible for who has access to the prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a rule only persons involved in the operation have access and in this case there were Tribunal people involved, and as far as I know -- rather, that they were present while this was going on in Room 331, and as far as I know this happened with the consent of the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: During the period between 5 o'clock and 7.30 were you continuously in Room 331, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not there throughout, because I also had other activities to carry out in connection with this operation. At 7.30 the interview began and I was present continuously as of about 9 o'clock, that is to say when the interview got to the part entitled about the case, and I was present from that point on until Mr. Mucic was brought to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So throughout the period 5.00 until 7.30 can you help me about this, please: Mr. Mucic was kept continuously in that room, is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know he was always in the room, but he may have been moved to the arrest cell at one point or another. If and when I can't recall, but at all events he wouldn't have been there for a long time because I was continuously after a short period coming back to the office and, as far as I can recall, he was always present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There was a German interpreter, an interpreter for the German language present throughout?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not a German interpreter. Rather, an interpreter for Croatian or Serbo-Croatian. This was the court sworn interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That was badly asked. An interpreter in order to interpret from the German language into Mr. Mucic's language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And your superior, Mr. Gschwendt, he was in there from time to time or all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Gschwendt was present in the office. Whether he was there from 5 o'clock until 1.15 in the morning, quite frankly I don't recall. He may have been out of the room at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The OTP representatives, were they in the room throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know that after the arrest and the searches, when we came to the offices the people from the Tribunal were not yet there. They arrived some time around 5.00 pm. It could have been a little later. At the time the interview began at 7.30, they were no longer present in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did they remain throughout that period in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During that period I was not always in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you returned on each occasion to the room, Room 331, Mr. Moerbauer, were they still there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were people from the Tribunal there. There was one, sometimes two people from the Tribunal, and we also went to the video room where the videos seized at Mucic's apartment, an attempt was made to copy them, and during that period I did go to -- back to the office, and when I did so, I did see people from the Tribunal there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with giving authority to the OTP representatives to speak to Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is it right that there were in total four people from the Office of the Prosecution, two investigators, an interpreter and a technical assistant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can recall that there was an interpreter along. Now, whether there were four people or altogether only three I don't recall the exact number. One person was with me in the video room. There may have been a second person of the Tribunal present in the video room with me, but as far as I can recall there should have been, yes, four people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Are there any rules in an extradition case, any rules in your criminal procedure about foreign police forces having access to prisoners, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, the involvement of the people of the Tribunal in this operation had received the consent of the investigating judge. I don't know what the grounds were, and I doubt that the investigating judge was breaking an Austrian law in doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you know the names of the people who were present in the room, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the names. I can only remember specifically the interpreter, but as far as the names go, I don't know the names of the other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, didn't you keep any sort of record who had access to this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether there's any note in the records about this. There may well have been a note entered into the record about this, but I didn't enter any such. It was entered in the report that on 20th March videotapes were handed over to representatives of the Tribunal, but other than that there is nothing in the documents I drew up about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did Austrian police officers remain in the room throughout, at least one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, as long as Mr. Mucic was in the room there was always an Austrian police officer in the room together with Mucic and the interpreter. That's what I saw each and every time I came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is that the team of four of you: yourself, Mr. Panzer, Mr. Bycek I think his name is and Mr. Borlak, one of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of the persons were present at one time or another. I recall that Mr. Panzer spent most of -- was the one who spent the most time in the office during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you know these three colleagues of yours very well, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spend a lot of time with Bycek, Panzer, etc. Borlak also, he spend a fair amount of time in our office as well, so I do spend a lot of time with these officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Are they fluent in English or are they English speaking, any of the three?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know Mr. Gschwendt speaks excellent English. Mr. Panzer speaks good English as well and Bycek speaks some English, enough to get by. With regard to Mr. Borlak, I don't know how much English he happens to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Does any of them know French?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Or Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Or Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None of these individuals speaks Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And also in that room, Room 331, were all the items that had been recovered and taken by the police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How big is Room 331, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 30-35 square metres approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And occupied, what, completely by desks or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are four desks there and there are some cabinets. Those are the objects that are in that room, but it was rather cramped when the people from the Tribunal were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Where was the seized material placed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The seized material was in that room in the containers in which they were brought there, that is to say that at that point in time they had not been locked into a cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: On one of the four desks or on more than one of the four desks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now whether they were on a desk or on the floor I can't really say. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So they hadn't been properly secured at that time. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was always someone in the room, so they had, in fact, been secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: They hadn't been put into a locked cabinet, had they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point in time not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Who exactly went to watch the videos of the people from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was a smaller gentleman with glasses, as best as I recall, but I'm afraid I can't give you his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did anybody go to watch with them, any of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As to whether a colleague was also along, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I asked you earlier about your prior knowledge of the case prior to interviewing this man. Did you get any further briefing from the representatives of the OTP prior to interviewing him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the Tribunal or from people of the Tribunal, no, I received no further information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did any of your colleagues who conducted the interviews receive any such briefing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So you were just going to rely on the short documents that you'd seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Now, at 7.30 in the evening the procedure of taking a statement from him was commenced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: By that stage he'd been at the very least up for some eight or nine hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And in the meantime he'd been arrested, his house had been searched and his 16 year old daughter had become involved in your investigation. He'd been taken to the police headquarters, detained and various formal procedures begun in respect of him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a nutshell, yes, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Apart from Mr. Mucic -- I'm sorry. Let me start that again. The document that was signed after midnight was signed by five people. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A number of documents were signed at the office after the arrest and then after the interview documents were signed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is that because all five people took part in the interview at some time or another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. It's for self-protection reasons that all the persons who participated in the interview signed the Niederschrift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I just want a clarification. When you talk about office, do you mean room number 331?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Room 331.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is it also this, that five people took part in the interviewing of Mr. Mucic at some time or another during the four and three-quarter hours that followed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now with regard to the questioning, the part about the individual was done by Borlak. The part about the case was done by myself. I put the questions via the interpreter and the three other individuals who signed the record were in the same room at certain periods of time during the interview, during the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Why did it need so many people to interview this one man, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The questioning was carried out by only two individuals, Mr. Borlak and myself, and it was on a one-on-one basis. Only Mr. Borlak and myself put questions to him. The other three persons who signed the record were in the room at the time and the interpreter signed the record as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So why did you need more than just yourself and your colleague to do this interview, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is done because often in trials it occurs that the accused at the trial says that he was hit during the questioning. This is why all the persons who were present during the questioning signed that record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, if you audio recorded or video recorded this interview, there would be no scope for such complaints, would there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But he said yesterday the video facility was not available in his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That was the answer to Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would like him to answer, please, if your Honour would be so kind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We do not have the technical facilities to make a video recording of such questions. We have a piece of video equipment, but we don't have a video camera, and that's not provided for, and I am not aware of video recordings of interviews being used in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is it normal to have four people interviewing a suspect in Austria, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. We have been having a procedure this afternoon that's quite irregular both for this Tribunal, as I understand it, and for the other courts in which I practised, where there seems to be two lawyers on one side bouncing up and down and making objections. It has been the procedure so far here, I think, and the procedure in every other court where I've ever practised that one lawyer handles one witness, presuming that the lawyer isn't disabled or something. Has there been a change in that practice or is it becoming a regular practice here? If it is, it's fine with me. I just want to find out what the procedure is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think it's even the procedure here. We've already indicated in this Trial Chamber that Mr. Grant Niemann is just coming into the picture. I think that's why it's happening. Ordinarily we have always stated here that you have the lead counsel. If he is in charge, he takes over. If the co-counsel is questioning, he is in charge. That's the procedure here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's what I thought, too. I just wanted to make sure I was correct in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Moerbauer, there were four people present in this room in order to intimidate him, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This witness was not intimidated. The only questioning was done by Borlak, the interpreter and at times the other persons were present in the room, and, in fact, we had a good basis for good discussion with Mr. Mucic and, as said, he was not intimidated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we'll go for a break now and come back at 4.30. (4.00 pm) (Short break) (4.30pm) (Witness re-enters court) (Interpreter re-enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. Mr. Moerbauer, what was the means of recording Mr. Mucic's statement, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The typewriter, that is to say text processing machine was used, that is to say you could see what was being written on the screen. The question was put via the interpreter to Mr. Mucic and then his answer and the question were written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Are we talking about a computer with a word processing programme or a dedicated word processor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a text processing typewriter with a screen where you can read along the whole page, and at the end of the interview, at the end of each page there's a print-out, and there's a possibility as regards the contents of storing it on a floppy disk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Apart from the record that was made obviously on the text processor, were any written notes made of the conversation which took place by anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is the possibility when the printed-out pages are submitted for signing that changes can be made in handwriting, and usually the line where a change is made, next to that line I think the signature is affixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That was not the question. Can a person make handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, no handwritten notes were added to the Niederschrift, the record. Interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm talking -- I'm sorry. I'm talking about notes quite separate from the record in the text processor. Were there any such notes made and, if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If possible simultaneous with the processor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing further was written. Now perhaps the interpreter might have made a few notes for translation purposes. I don't know. But with regard to the questioning, that went into the text processing machine and no other notes were made by the police in relation to this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The record of that interview that you signed and have identified, is that a verbatim account of what was said by the questioner and Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I put the question to him in German. The interpreter translated the question, and the reply by Mr. Mucic was in its native tongue, and the interpreter translated that back into German, and then that was typed into the Niederschrift, the record of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is that the procedure that is adopted by all of your colleagues in recording an interview of this kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the same procedure that's used, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So that all the words that are recorded and set out in that statement, those are in their entirety all the words of Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The wording in the record is the translation provided by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let's just get this absolutely clear. Do you understand the word "verbatim"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is written up in the form in which it is given by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let's just move on to this point, please, Mr. Moerbauer. Bearing in mind that by the time the interview started he'd been up for some eight or nine hours and had been in custody for four and three quarter hours, did you or any of your colleagues at any time during the course of that interview enquire whether he was tired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question whether he was tired, I don't know whether it was put to him by colleagues. I didn't put it to him, but he was asked whether he would like something to eat or something to drink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just one question here. What was appearing on the screen was in German?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So he had no opportunity to see what was coming up on the screen, because he doesn't know German himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now on the screen all that is indeed in German. Then there's a print-out. Then that's translated back by the interpreter, and after that the person questioned has to sign each and every page of the Niederschrift, of the record of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that the interview continued on into the early hours of the morning of 19th March, Mr. Moerbauer, why didn't you enquire if he was tired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic was given the possibility to state his views about the charges against him, and it might actually have led to a shortening of the time he might have spent in custody, because this is passed on to the judge and he might have applied for release from custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Now would you like to answer the question that I asked you, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You did not ask him whether he was tired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That question was not put to him and at no point in time during the interview did he say he was tired. It was only at the end of the interview that he said that he was tired, and that's when at all events he was being brought to police custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What counsel is saying, that he has been on for so long in the interview, why did you not ask him whether he was tired, because he'd spent a long time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't consider the possibility that he might be tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You ignored --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose that's your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So during the course of that interview it never occurred to you, this interview which had lasted four and three quarter hours, that he might be tired at all. You'd never considered that possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time no. All of us were pretty tired, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Quite, Mr. Moerbauer. He was bound to be tired, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He must have been tired, yes. That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You carried on this interview regardless of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic was interviewed with a view to possibly shortening the time he might spend in custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So by interviewing him for four and three quarter hours until he's very tired, you might help him to shorten his time in custody. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The time in custody might have been shortened if in the course of the interview it emerged that there were no grounds for arrest. The contents, or rather the record of the interview itself was passed on to the judge the next day, so on that basis the judge could have decided to terminate or shorten the period of custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And so the fact that the contents were going to be passed on to the investigating judge, that makes it all right for you to carry on interviewing a man even when he's very tired. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The arrested person, according to the Code of Criminal Procedure, is to be questioned in relation to the grounds for his arrest, and that's what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And that's the Austrian law, isn't it, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Austrian law it says that he is to be questioned in regard to the reasons of arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The document that was signed, it was signed by all of you, you and your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The record was signed by all of the persons who were present at one point in time or another during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And by signing it, you are taking responsibility for the entire document, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By signing it, what is happening is you are ascertaining that those people were present at the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you read it before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The document was read through and it was written in part by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
