utterances.text: Would your Honour just give me a moment please? One of the sections in the interview, Mr. Moerbauer, was to establish his personal circumstances, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Amongst the information that you were able to establish, did you establish whether or not he was qualified in Austrian law at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not conduct the part of the interview entitled "about the individual". I took over at the part that begins about the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, but you read through the record of the interview. Did any part of that suggest that he was qualified in Austrian law, and in particular in criminal law and procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regarding any qualification, I don't believe there's anything in the record about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you help us as to how Mr. Mucic might have said to your colleague that the search warrant and arrest warrant were lawful ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, how the colleague went about this is something I can't comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just remind us of the name of the man who was conducting that part of the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question about the individual was conducted by my colleague Borlak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And you've told us that the procedure means that everything which is said by the accused man, the suspect, that's what gets into the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a rule everything is taken down. Now in this case it was on a question by question basis, and when a question was answered, the answer was written down in the Niederschrift.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Moerbauer, I suggest that at the end of the interview you failed to warn him of his right to correct any mistakes, although you may well have told him he could add anything. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a rule for each and every individual, for every record, every suspect is -- everyone who is questioned has the possibility to make changes or additions. The interpreter was certainly told by me to tell him that. As regards the extent to which she did so, I can't say, but, as said, she was a court sworn interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You see, what I suggest to you is that the record you have produced is, in fact, not an accurate record of what was said by Mr. Mucic, and that at the end of the interview when he read the document over, he asked to correct something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember anything along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He was by now a man who was desperately tired, I suggest to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible that he was tired. We were all quite tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When he read the document over, he did want to correct something I suggest to you, Mr. Moerbauer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware that Mr. Mucic wanted to change anything in the record of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, I go further than that. I suggest that you simply refused to allow a correction, and told him he would get out of the place quicker if he signed it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You never gave him any food. You never gave him any drinks. You never offered him any breaks in the interview, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not true. Mr. Mucic was given something to drink. He didn't want anything to eat and at the end of the interview a colleague gave him a sandwich and an apple.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just help me about this. Did you know what was being interpreted by the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only say I put the questions. As regards the answers -- let me go back a bit. The questions were translated by the interpreter. Mr. Mucic's answers were translated by the interpreter, and then that's what was written down in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you check the record to see if it accorded with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The record was read once again on the screen. I have the whole page before me. There is sometimes mistakes, typing mistakes. Those are corrected. Then there's the print-out. I read it. The interpreter translates it and gives it to the interviewee for signing. That's the procedure and that's what happened in this instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would like to move on, please, to 20th March, when you permitted a lawyer from the Office of the Prosecution to speak to the investigating judge -- do you recall that -- either of the Tribunal or of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think you told us either yesterday or the day before about an Afrikaner lawyer with a surname called Dutoit. Do you remember recording a conversation over the telephone with the judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on 20th March. Mr. Dutoit of the Tribunal was at our office and he was given the videotapes that had been seized. This was after consultation with Dr. Seda, the investigating judge, and that consultation took place by colleague Bycek over the phone. Mr. Dutoit also spoke via the telephone with Dr. Seda. Bycek wanted a written confirmation about the conversation with the investigating judge. The latter declined for time reasons, and in this regard Mr. Bycek drew up a note. He made an entry in the record. As far as I know, Mr. Dutoit was not a lawyer but an investigator.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not quite hear whether Mr. Moerbauer was present at that -- he was present at that phone call by his colleague, Bycek.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No doubt my colleagues for the Prosecution can tell us what Mr. Dutoit's status is, but you permitted this man to make representations to the judge, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Dutoit spoke to the judge over the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was the conversation in English or German?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't quite remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mucic informed of this conversation, Mr. Moerbauer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no further contact with Mr. Mucic after he was transferred to the prison on the 19th. As to whether he was informed of that conversation or not, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And you can't say whether he was given an opportunity himself to address the judge in the way that the Tribunal's representative had been able to; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With regard to that conversation, I do not know, but in the course of the interview Mr. Mucic was informed that the following day, that is to say on 19th March, there would be questioning by the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would Mr. Mucic have been allowed to speak to the judge in the way that the Tribunal's representative was, if he'd asked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic had the conversation or, shall we say, that conversation on 19th March.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you consider it was fair to have allowed the Tribunal's representative to speak to the judge when Mr. Mucic wasn't going to be able to do so or know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a decision by the investigating judge and the decisions of the investigating judge were simply taken note of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: My final question is this, Mr. Moerbauer. As far as the documents which were recovered on 18th March were concerned, you confirmed that not one of them was ever analysed by way of handwriting expert examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the part of the police, that is to say the Vienna Police Department, no such handwriting analysis was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So all that you can say is that so many documents were recovered, and you can say nothing about the authorship of any one of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could put it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As far as matters of continuity are concerned, I adopt the cross-examination of my learned friend Ms. Residovic and I have no further questions. Thank you very much, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know this will pain everyone in the courtroom, but I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We anticipated you would have none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just one question. What time did you lock up all the papers and the videos you had collected and Panzer had collected and Unger had collected and Mr. Navrat had handed them over to you? What time did you lock them up in your cabinet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was prior to Mr. Mucic's transfer to the prison facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is about 1.30 am?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 1 o'clock, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no further questions for re-examination. We only have to talk about then our tendering of exhibits for the time being. As I already stated before, we seek to tender now for the time being the exhibits -- well, first of all, we have to go back to our original intention as far as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I have a simple question to ask. Now you said at the conclusion all of you were tired, including yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually at what stage did you feel that tiredness, both yourself and the person being questioned, because you admitted you were all tired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was tired, well, it was in the evening hours. An interview, keeping a record, it's a very tiring business. Towards the end of the interview I dare say I was quite tired indeed, but it's not -- it wasn't to the point that I didn't know what I was saying or what I was doing. I still had myself under control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: But you continued with the exercise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were only questions in respect of which Mr. Mucic could give his point of view and, as said, his answers might well have shortened his period of custody. An attempt was made to give him an opportunity to understand the grounds of arrest with the possibility also of doing away with those grounds, making them unfounded, and the outcome of that interview was transmitted to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you at any stage he was tired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the interview was over he did say yes, he was tired, and that's also when he was taken into the police prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: As I was telling, the Prosecution has to go back to its original intention of tendering for admission also the big document numbered as number 104, the report, the index, for the simple reason that the witness was challenged as to the capability of him -- of identifying the seized documents one by one. We want to emphasise anyway that we seek to tender this document not for the truth of the single Ausvertung, the single analysis, the evaluation of the single documents. We only want to tender this document because it shows the system for identifying the documents which this witness could follow. It will show the grounds on which he could actually be in a position of identifying every single document for the simple reason that the numbering of the documents inside every file was reflected in this report. So this is why we are going to tender this document for admission. Furthermore, of course the witness signed the documents in every subsection. Then we tender for admission documents 105, 106, 107 and 108 for the time being, which are the two passports seized by this witness in the apartment of Mr. Mucic, the pass for the War Presidency in the name of Mr. Mucic, 107, and the military ID card of HVO of Mr. Mucic, which is 108. Then we tender for admission the police interview numbered as 145 and, of course, we tender for admission the search record numbered as 151, which is the search record concerning the house search in the apartment of Mr. Mucic, which was carried on personally by Mr. Moerbauer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems to me that the Prosecution has -- I don't know -- three or four additional witnesses that they are now bringing with regard to all these matters. It seems to me the appropriate time for the Prosecution to tender documents for admission and for the defence to respond is after we've heard all the witnesses rather than doing a kind of piecemeal at the close of direct, at the close of cross with every witness, trying to tender things. This is all intertwined. I think it all ought to be handled at once. Then the court could hear all the arguments at once and deal with it all at once. That's just a suggestion on procedure, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Turone, you remember you have given an undertaking that many of these documents can only be tendered through some of the subsequent witnesses you are calling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. All the other documents, but these few documents are not connected to either the search in Inda-Bau or the search in Delalic's apartment, and this is why we thought that only these few documents are not connected with the matter which must be covered by the other police -- the Austrian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Are some of these documents not from the bag in which the documents were brought?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The four documents, 105-107, were seized by Mr. Moerbauer personally in the apartment of Mr. Mucic, and so they have nothing to do with the search in Inda-Bau and with the house search in the apartment of Mr. Delalic. This is why we are for the time being talking about four seized documents only, because these four seized documents are not connected to anything which has to be asked to future witnesses belonging to the Austrian police. This is the reason why we -- our intention, our submission, is to tender immediately these few documents for the time being, leaving all the rest of the about 47 numbered exhibits, numbered items, to the future. This is our submission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic? MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. In this phase of the proceedings I contest the approach of my learned colleague on the Prosecution. He's trying to put together a mosaic which is not relevant at this stage, while all the controlling facts regarding the testimony of this witness are still to be investigated through other witnesses that will be brought by the Prosecution, so that this piecemeal presentation of evidence I think is not appropriate, and the defence of Mr. Mucic strongly objects to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moran?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I have a problem with Exhibit 104. That thing is full of: "This document means that". "This document means something else". It's full of references to documents that I haven't seen that surely aren't part of the record of this trial. Judge, it's just not relevant, or at least a lot of it in there is not relevant. The Prosecution wants to attempt to redact it, to redact out the opinion, to redact out references to documents that haven't been presented to the court, that type of thing, it would be a different story, but right now that document's just full from front to back of things that are irrelevant and probably even if they were relevant, would be inadmissible in any case. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I should like to join my learned colleagues in their objections and to say that I object to any of the tendered documents being admitted as evidence. Regarding the submission for the acceptance of various reports listed under point -- registered under 104, these are police reports. They are analyses of evidence which are not part of the court file. For this very reason they are inadmissible as evidence. On the other hand, in a very thick part of the file are reports signed by various persons and not just by this witness, and therefore for that reason too they are inadmissible and premature. Finally, they contain a number of illogical allegations which will probably be removed later on in the proceedings. However, regardless of that, I think that the police records cannot be partially evidence, as proposed by colleague Turone, whereas they would not be admitted as evidence for some other things. I also object to admitting as evidence other objects offered, registered under 105, 106, 107, 108, 145 and 151, since in the course of the testimony of this witness it has been established without any doubt that in the case of the search of Mr. Mucic's apartment, attended by this witness, a number of irregularities occurred and unlawful acts according to the Austrian law, ranging from the date on the Protokoll, the facts contained in that Protokoll, the fact that it was not signed on the spot, but later on in the police station and so on. Therefore, these documents, too, in the collection of which this witness participated, though he apparently was in five different places at the same time, we feel that this is sufficient ground not to admit these documents as evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you wish to make a reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, my first preliminary reply is that tendering of documents is often done in a kind of a piecemeal fashion, because it depends upon the way the case is going on. So I would like -- may I ask your Honour if your Honours think that this tendering in a piecemeal fashion is possible, then I will go on and give my arguments in response to what I heard my esteemed colleagues from the defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually you can only tender documents through a witness if he is capable of showing his relationship to that document and how it came to be in existence. If you can show that and without any ambiguity, then you might be able to tender them, but if it's not certain that he could have produced a document or it was never in his custody, it might be difficult for you to do so. So you now try to tender those documents which you think are related to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Exactly, your Honour. My intention is to tender these few documents right now, because I believe that these documents can be tendered through this witness for the reasons which I might explain to your Honours, if you wish, today. If you allow me, I will explain my arguments in response to the defence lawyers now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hear you in respect of those documents you think this witness can tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, as I told already to Mr. -- concerning Mr. Moran's objections on document 104, our intention is not to tender this document, to enter this document into evidence as for the truth of every single analysis and evaluation it contains concerning the single documents it describes. It is our submission that this document shows exactly the system the witness followed to classify and study the documents so that it may explain correctly the reason why he is in a position -- he has been in a position to recognise and identify one by one the documents which was submitted to him thanks to the fact that in that report every single file was reflected and the numbering of every single document inside every single file was also reflected, and that is why the witness could -- was in a position to identify those documents. So it is not only an aide memoire, but it is something which now gives us the possibility to show how this witness was actually in a position to do that recognition. On the other hand, we would say in a very general way that Rule 73 requires that an accused who wishes to exclude evidence obtained from him make a motion to that effect preliminarily and in any event prior to trial. Mr. Delalic did this and was unsuccessful. With respect to all evidence seized in Vienna, Mr. Delalic's objections have been ruled on. Surely it's our submission that Rule 73 must have a point to it such that absent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, without interrupting you, that is not the only exclusionary Rule. There are others. You still have Rule 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I'm going to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do not dwell so much on a matter which is not completely concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going also to this point later on, but if you allow me to present all our arguments, I would be grateful to you. Anyway, I know that Rule 73 is not the only Rule applying in these cases, but may I proceed, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, you can proceed, but I wouldn't like you to proceed on the wrong foot when, in fact, you know that finally evidence can be excluded if other conditions apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Let me go ahead then, your Honour. Even if the accused had brought any challenges timely, however these objections must anyway fail as set out in Rule 89A. This Tribunal is not bound by national laws or rules, but instead is entitled to consider any relevant evidence, as long as it was not obtained by means contrary to internationally protected human rights, or its admission would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. For many different reasons this Tribunal does not have strict evidence rules. Instead we believe that questions of admissibility are for the Chamber to decide based on all the circumstances. What may or may not be required or even common in various jurisdictions are not controlling here. So both the search of Mr. Mucic's apartment and the statement were obtained fairly and should be admitted, in our opinion, as relevant evidence. Of course, the Trial Chamber shall determine what weight they should be given, depending on the actual material as well as the circumstances. Let's say something on the scope of the search warrant. The search warrant has a very general wording, too. It says about objects, the possession or sight of which could be significant for the proceedings in question. In the search warrant the judge says: "Documents about war crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina". This is a general expression indicating any document which might be relevant for the future investigation and prosecution of war crimes, even if they don't show directly a specific war crime having been committed. Even as for tortures, the search warrant says in particular the search seeks to find out anything concerning directly torture, but this does not -- this means that the general expression "objects the possession or sight of which could be significant for the proceedings", documents about war crimes. These general expressions are not nullified by this particular mention in the search warrants. Since the position of the accused inside the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and their possible command responsibility are an issue strictly connected to the matter of the war crimes for which they are accused, any document showing their position in the armed forces which was lawfully seized within the scope of the search warrant is admissible, in our submission. This applies to documents 107 and 108 in particular, which show Mr. Mucic's possibility to enter the premises of the war presidency and his position inside HVO. The two passports are relevant not only for the relationship itself between Mr. Mucic and the apartment in which they were seized, but also for some -- with respect to his alibi defence, which implies at least an alleged trip of Mr. Mucic outside the former Yugoslavia in the period of time relevant for this trial, and I emphasise that both passports were valid for 1992. Briefly, the search of Mucic's apartment was done lawfully, in our submission. The police were directed to search Mr. Mucic's apartment by an investigating magistrate pursuant to this search warrant. The police, including Mr. Moerbauer, did so. Certain documents were seized, and the Prosecution has tendered them into evidence. I was saying the search was ordered and executed lawfully. The fact itself that there may have been some technical issues such as the age of the witnesses, for instance, cannot seriously be argued to rise to the level that the admission would seriously undermine the integrity of the proceedings and, indeed, although it is not controlling the Prosecution would note that such would not even be a reason to challenge its admissibility in Austrian courts, and much less in international courts. The provisions argued by the defence could have been violated deal with the manner and way the searches are executed, but do not affect the result or their admissibility at trial. If your Honours wish, our colleague Mr. Stefan Waespi, who has some knowledge of Austrian and international law, better than I, could argue this and provide supporting case law and legal argument. Anyway in the absence of a specific request from your Honours, we would not plan on presenting such further arguments, because it is for us even hardly or scarcely relevant, but if your Honours wish, Mr. Stefan Waespi will be able to give some more legal arguments like that. What is relevant, finally, and I conclude, is the simple question: is the evidence relevant? To this I think everyone must concede yes. Whether consideration of the evidence somehow offends Rule 95, again the answer must be yes. Well, was the search perfect? Well, I would say no. What you have had is a search of numerous locations and an arrest. Because of operational matters everything had to happen earlier than expected. A large amount of material was seized, hundreds of documents and numerous videos. Yes, there were mistakes. Yes, that is a problem. Yes, it is regrettable, but can it be seriously argued that the mistakes constitute violations of fundamental human rights? Can it seriously be argued that the admission of the evidence would seriously damage the integrity of these proceedings? We would say no. At the end, last point, the interview of Mr. Mucic, the statement was taken fairly. Mr. Mucic was advised of his rights, including his right to remain silent, his right to consult an attorney. There was a certified interpreter. Mr. Mucic chose to speak. He was advised of certain facts, which include two non-controversial facts, that if he chose to remain silent he would not be able to give his side of the story and, second, that if he cooperated and was later found guilty the cooperation could be considered mitigation. These facts are true according to Austrian law, and it cannot be argued that telling someone what the law says constitutes improper or unfair inducement. The Prosecution would also note that most systems, including that of this Tribunal, have similar provision in their law. We can then -- we can later provide your Honours with case law from the European Court of Human Rights demonstrating that these warnings are perfectly consistent with the code of human rights. These are my arguments. As I said, if your Honours desire, Mr. Stefan Waespi will have further legal arguments of Austrian and international law. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Which are the documents you want to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: As I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Spell them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: As I said, 104, which is the big report, index, not for the truth of the single analysis, but for the system the witness followed to classify documents and for the way through which he could identify them one by one in this courtroom, 104. Number 105 and 106, the two passports of Mucic seized by Mr. Moerbauer in the apartment of Mucic, which were valid in 1992. 107 and 108, two ID cards having relevancy as for the position of Mr. Mucic in the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Number 148, the police interview, the record of the police interview of Mr. Mucic done starting at 7.30 on March 18th and, last, number 151, which is the search record, the house search record concerning the apartment of Mr. Mucic, which was signed by Mr. Moerbauer, who carried on personally the house search together with three other colleagues. All these documents we believe are not connected at all with what other witnesses from Austrian police will have to say in this courtroom in the next few days. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Don't you see that different principles govern different documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Our submission is that these documents are not affected by the issues which must be covered by the other witnesses of the police of Vienna in the next days. This is our submission, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There are five documents which you want to be tendered in evidence. The first is an analysis of all the documents seized from different locations. His analysis is his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: As I said, your Honour, we are trying to enter this document into evidence not for the truth of the single -- of the analysis of every single document. This applies also to -- some defence lawyer requested the redaction of this document. We believe that a redaction of such a document is not necessary simply because this is not a trial by jury and professional judges are in a position to sift every single piece of evidence and give the concerned value to each one of them, but anyway our intention is to tender this document into evidence not for the content of the single evaluations; just because of the numbering which is reflected in this document and is directly connected with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But how is numbering relevant? How is that numbering relevant? What is its probative value.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is its probative value? The test is relevancy and probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We do not consider this document to enter into evidence because of the content of every single analysis, but simply because it is a complex document, official documents, with signatures of this witness, and it gives the real idea of how this witness proceeded in the handling of these documents, in the classification of these documents and proves how documents could be identified by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This witness is capable of tendering them because he has indicated a system through which he did them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This is the reason and another reason is that this witness signed this document, so it is a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He might have signed thousands of documents but show us the relevancy of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. This is also part of the chain. It goes to the chain, too. It proves how documents can be identified and it goes to the chain of custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Identified for what purpose? Show us the relevancy -- the probative value of this document, why you want to bury the record with documents which have no probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this documentary reflects exactly what the witness said as for the classification and numbering of the single documents he could identify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But he has already explained what he has done, but why have that document on the record? He has told us how he classified these documents, but what is its probative value, apart from showing us his method which he has already explained?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Because there was some challenging of this witness as for the numbering of the single documents inside every file, and since this numbering of the documents inside every file is reflected in the report, we believe that this report might be useful in order to give a better idea of the system followed by the witness, which allowed this witness to identify documents one by one. This is our reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How are the passports relevant? He had -- nobody is saying that Mr. Mucic had no access to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The passports might be relevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is the case of the defence that he had no access to Bosnia-Herzegovina during the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The two passports, your Honour, are valid in the period of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are producing them to show that he had access to the area of conflict. There is nothing more than that, or is there any other purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: There is a defence of alibi of Mr. Mucic concerning also travels outside Yugoslavia in the relevant period of time. So these documents may be relevant in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: To rebut a plea of alibi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As regards his police statement, you have just mentioned that he was informed of his rights of having a counsel, but I think Mr. Gschwendt probably said that right to have a counsel was not available but he was being interviewed by the police. That is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. This is one of the items Mr. Stefan Waespi might cover in further legal argument, whenever your Honours deem that useful, if your Honour deemed that useful. Thank you. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, may I speak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you wish to discuss anything? Do you want to make any contribution? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us hear it. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you. First of all, I think that the question of admissibility of these documents is premature. The Prosecution has already proposed and the Trial Chamber has ruled that it will decide on the admissibility of all the exhibits after hearing the witnesses that the Prosecution intends to call. However, your Honours, in addition to that, I wish to apologise to our learned colleagues on the side of the Prosecution, but I think that in the arguments they have offered they are not acting in accordance with -- not acting in a way that could be described as correct by referring to certain rules of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence and to the claim that the rules of a national legislation cannot be applied. I must say that the only system that is in accordance with Article 29 of the Statute regarding house searches and the search and seizure of objects that can be applied is the Criminal Code of Procedure of Austria, as the country which cooperates with the Tribunal, which assists the Tribunal, and which has acted in every way in accordance with Article 29.2 of the Statute of the International Tribunal. Therefore, any attempt to interpret Rule 89B of our rules in any other way in my view is not in accordance with the law of this Tribunal, nor does it strengthen the lawful proceedings in this Tribunal. Both witnesses said that any unlawfulness in the collection of evidence calls in question the acceptance of that evidence. Also I think that the attempt of the Prosecution to try and tender these exhibits as evidence which is premature, let me say again. In doing so they wish to draw attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that the objections of the defence of Mr. Zejnil Delalic have been rejected. In fact, they are referring to the court Ruling of October 1996, in which it was clearly stated that objects are not returned to the accused, that the Prosecution may use them in preparation for the proceedings, but as to the admissibility of the evidence, that is decided when that evidence is tendered in the proceedings. For these reasons, as well as the reasons given before, it is my claim that it is unacceptable to admit as evidence the reports of the police and notes of policemen analysing those reports, which in the view of the Prosecution itself has no probative value regarding the case. I also think that evidence cannot be tendered which would only provide 5 per cent of the evidence proving a link regarding the lawfulness of the collection of evidence, because the chain, the chain of command can only be confirmed by the witnesses. This witness said what he knew. The other witnesses will show us the chain of custody regarding the way in which evidence was collected. I wish to remind the Trial Chamber that this morning this witness recognised only one document which he had analysed and not seized during his search. To offer indirectly through item 104 the verification of lawfulness which is being disputed is neither timely nor is it proper and that is why I propose that the Trial Chamber assess the lawfulness of the procedure at the end of the presentation of evidence, because any unlawfulness can annul the validity of the evidence, and I think only then can any ruling be made on the admissibility of individual exhibits as evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually I thought it has been understood that this witness is only tendering those documents he can tender. He's not dealing with documents which other witnesses might still come in to tender. So I don't see why you are spreading the net so wide, including those who are not here, whose relationship to the documents are not involved here. We are only dealing with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why can't he produce those documents which he himself received from Mucic's apartment? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, document 104 refers to thousands of documents, and I do not know why it is being tendered at all as evidence. Some of those the defence may never have seen. Under 104 there is reference to documents and reports that were not drawn up by this witness. There are documents there that the witness says were signed by someone else on his behalf. Actually somebody had forged his signature. The Prosecutor is offering us this document 104 as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge, let me put on my amicus hat for just a second, because I really don't have a dog in this fight. There has been a couple of things that have been said by the Prosecution and I keep hearing it over and over and over and I think somebody needs to talk a little bit about it, where they say: "Because you are all trained judges, we can just shove in any kind of evidence we want to in here and let you all sort it out later". We do have Rules of Evidence in this Tribunal. Rules of Evidence were adopted by the Tribunal, by the court, admittedly not nearly as restrictive as you might find in some national rules of evidence, but we do have rules of evidence. Right up at the top Rule 89C says you may admit relevant evidence. Well, you've got to start off with that, which it would seem to me would say you don't admit anything that's irrelevant. There are other rules for exclusion of evidence throughout our Rules of Procedure. The Tadic case we have talked about dear knows how many times. It has to have some kind of reliability. It has to have some kind of probative value that's shown outside of itself. Judge, I think at some point the Prosecution ought to -- we ought all to stop saying: "Because we have trained judges here, we can just shove in anything we want and the judges will sort it out later". I think we do have rules of evidence and they need to be followed. You cannot get around them just by that simple matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might add just a word. I know I have been silent for many months now. There are also two issues on the admissibility of these documents we are talking about. One is just the basic ability to authenticate them as reliable. The other issue that I believe my learned colleague Ms. Residovic is referring to is she has a motion to suppress that was validly filed whether these were admissible as appropriately seized under the laws of Vienna. Until that issue has been resolved, you can't get them in because maybe they think they have been authenticated. There is still the question of whether there has been legality of search and seizure in that area. All the witnesses have not come forward to present evidence as to whether that was legally seized at that time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you want to say anything? Do you have any contribution? MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. Very briefly, your Honours, in the response of our learned colleague on the side of the Prosecution, he did not say anything essential that is also relevant except for one thesis, which we will be discussing at length, and that is the question of objective responsibility, Article 7.3. Of course, he tried to do that in order to provide more argument for his submission, but those arguments do not stand, namely I do not see why we should at this stage of the proceedings, when we will yet be hearing other witnesses, and then these exhibits can be tendered as evidence, why is the Prosecution insisting so much on tendering such evidence which, to put it mildly, is incorrect in relation to the defence, because my colleague, pursuant to Article 95, after the 90 day period, initiated this proceedings that we are in now. Therefore, the argument of my learned colleague will not be affected by hearing at least three more witnesses, if not more, and then if there are grounds, then this will certainly be admitted as evidence. I, therefore, consider this submission to be irrelevant at this point, that is to make these exhibits evidence now. I would propose that it be done at a later stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just make a very brief comment about Exhibit 104? It will just take me a second. The Prosecution suggest that that is now admissible because it explains the witness' document numbering system. If the Prosecution thought there was some confusion about that, they had an opportunity to clear it up on re-examination of the witness. Instead of excepting re-examination and trying to make it clear, if they think it's not clear, they have offered this document, which contains a lot of irrelevant material beyond explaining his numbering system. It is kind of needing to define the word "dog" offering the entire dictionary because it is in there somewhere. I think it is inappropriate they couldn't clear it up on some additional cross-examination and take care of it that way and it is not a document that's filled with all of these irrelevancies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will give a ruling tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Could I just mention one matter which is not to do with this. The Prosecution promised us a revised witness list some time ago. We have never received it. We still do need to prepare our cases with the future in mind. Please could the Prosecution provide us with the revised witness list in the light of the events of about two weeks ago, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, you gave that undertaking that you can produce the precise lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We have told the defence and the Chamber that we will provide a revised witness list as soon as we're able to, and we are, for instance, with respect to the witnesses that are going to appear this week, we've told them those. With respect to any other witnesses, in terms of the specific order, we're unable now to know it, because it depends -- because, to be frank, the old witness list is not so out of date in terms of timing and the witnesses' schedule that that is not possible. We are working with the Victim Witness Unit trying to get in contact with the witnesses and see when they appear. Obviously when things come up, such as the fact that we are now going to call more Austrian police officers than we had anticipated, that also puts things back. It is also the case that certain witnesses have, at least as of now, refused now to come because of the events of the last few weeks. We are continuing our efforts to potentially try to convince some of them to once again come. So other than to say that we will tell them as soon as we know anything, and, for instance, we told them last week about the witnesses this week, I'm afraid we can't give any more detail, but certainly we will do everything possible to give people notice. I'm also supposed to ask just to confirm that this witness may be excused today. He's scheduled to go back. I also don't believe we have an interpreter in any event and I believe cross-examination is finished. So I just formally ask that this witness be excused before we recess. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, you now see the position which everybody hears. I think it depends on the availability of the witnesses, the persons they can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It was not really availability I was concerned about. I wanted to know who is not now coming. You then discard those and you don't concentrate on those. Otherwise I end up just doing things that are useless and pointless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose the Prosecution will still make efforts to see how you can facilitate the defence's anxiety. It might be difficult for them to keep on not knowing what to face, because, as it is now, they do not know what to do next.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, we try to tell them in enough time so that they can prepare. The Prosecution could potentially give an idea of which witnesses we now don't think will come, but we're reluctant to do that, because if next week the witness changes their mind for some reason, I am afraid the defence might then object and say: "Oh, no, you told us this witness wasn't coming". Other than to say we will tell them in sufficient notice, as we have been, for the next couple of weeks, at least we have to know that, because the Victim Witness Unit has to make the arrangements, I think at this point we are unable to do more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As I've just said, we'll give our ruling on the submissions tomorrow morning. This witness is discharged. So we will adjourn until tomorrow morning at 10.00. (6.00 pm)
